Q: Flutter SocketException when using USB debugging A:

In the Android folder I opened the gradle-wrapper.properties file, found the version Flutter is trying to use, opened an Android project in Android Studio and changed the project's Gradle version to that of Flutter and let Android Studio download the Gradle. I reopened my Flutter project; it downloaded some files and everything worked.

Sometimes Android Studio does not download the Gradle. Just set your preferred Gradle, go to gradle-wrapper.properties in the Android Studio project and delete the backslash from the distribution URL (make sure the URL is correct). Then invalidate the cache and restart.

Sometimes Android Studio is not able to download the lower version Gradle that Fluter uses. Just copy the URL of the current Android Studio Gradle which should have been downloaded at the time, copy the URL and paste it in the Flutter project's gradle-wrapper.properties on the distribution URL. It will download the necessary file and should work.

Q: CUDA driver version is insufficient for CUDA runtime version A:

  1. Install TensorFlow version 1.14, installing Keras

  2. Install CUDA 10.0 from https://developer.nvidia.com/cuda-10.0-download-archive?target_os=Windows&target_arch=x86_64&target_version=10&target_type=exenetwork for windows

  3. Download the compatible CuDNN i.e 7.4.2 from https://developer.nvidia.com/rdp/cudnn-archive

  4. set the following in the path variable

    • cudnn-10.0-windows10-x64-v7.4.2.24\cuda\bin
    • cudnn-10.0-windows10-x64-v7.4.2.24\cuda\include
    • cudnn-10.0-windows10-x64-v7.4.2.24\cuda\lib\x64

  5. Restart the PC

Q: Why does sorting reduces the time of my function? A:

Why sort speeds up readarray : A case of I/O Serialization complexity and system overhead

While sort adds O(n log n) operations, it solves a massive bottleneck in how Bash manages memory and process synchronization.

The Slow Path :

 When  you run
 (seq 0 20000) readarray -t array ; 
 two processes are fighting for resources.

  1. The Producer(seq): Floods the pipe buffer immediately.

  2. The Consumer(readarray): Must wake up, read a line, allocate memory(via malloc) and store it.

Because Bash is an interpreted shell it memory management is relatively slow. In this scenario, the kernel is constantly context switching between the producer and the consumer. Every time seq fills a bit of the pipe, readarray tries to empty it. The Handshaking creates massive overhead that far outweighs the actual data processing.

The Faster Path :

 When  you run
 (seq 0 20000|sort) readarray -t array;
 two processes are fighting for resources.

Adding sort changes the architecture from streaming to batching.

  1. The Dam Effect: sort is a "blocking" utility. It cannot output anything until it has read the very last line (EOF) because it doesn't know which line come first until the end.

  2. Serialization : While sort is running, readarray is blocked and idle. This eliminates context switching during the "Collection" phase. sort (Written in Highly optimized C) handles 20000 lines in its own internal memory space much faster than Bash can.

  3. Efficient Ingestion: Once sort finishes, it flushes its entire result set into the pipe at once. readarray then reads this data in large, contiguous bursts. The kernel can pass the data through the pipe much more efficiently because the "producer" (sort) is now just dumping a finished buffer rather than generating lines one by one.

Q: What does "int 0x80" mean in assembly code? A:

What does the following assembly code do? int 0x80

The code line (string) "

 int 0x80

"

instructs the assembler to produce the two machine code bytes CD 80 (in hexadecimal), and then the assembler will move to the next line, without the need (for the assembler) to do anything else in that regard. That's a pretty simple instruction from the assembler point of view.

What Intel says its processor does is written in Intel 64 and IA-32 Architectures Software Developer’s Manual Combined Volumes: 1, 2A, 2B, 2C, 2D, 3A, 3B, 3C, 3D, and 4

  • briefly in the Section 6.5.4 INT n, INTO, INT3, INT1, and BOUND Instructions (Volume 1) (see the whole Chapter 6: PROCEDURE CALLS, INTERRUPTS, AND EXCEPTIONS)
  • with great detail in INT n/INTO/INT3/INT1—Call to Interrupt Procedure (Vol. 2A 3-524, page 1114 of the cumulative pdf) this precisely answer to "what does" from the CPU point of view.
  • briefly Vol. 3A CHAPTER 7: INTERRUPT AND EXCEPTION HANDLING (from page 3267 of the pdf and don't miss the last page of the chapter Interrupts 32 to 255—User Defined Interrupts (7-58 Vol. 3A)
  • Vol. 3B 22-17 22.3.3 Class 3—Software Interrupt Handling in Virtual-8086 Mode if that's your context

Other answers focused on what the processor is assumed to do after, but in regard to int 80h nowadays it likely depends on how the OS/distribution chose to support 32vcbit in 64 bit (AMD64) architecture, the instruction (0f 05) syscall should be used instead to interact with 64-bit Unix-like OSes (for example, for an overview of syscall in OpenBSD, see the files that were generated by makesyscalls.sh and syscalls.master, handled by mi_syscall, mostly reached by the syscall instruction (in x86 not opcode cd 80 but 0f 05) in syscall function in the C library:

objdump-sub /usr/lib/libc.so.84.2 syscall

Output:

objdump -d --start-address=0x0000000000090430 --stop-address=$((0x0000000000090430+0x000000000000000d)) /usr/lib/libc.so.84.2

/usr/lib/libc.so.96.0:     file format elf64-x86-64

Disassembly of section .text:

00000000000b26e0 <_thread_sys___syscall>:
   b26e0:       b8 c6 00 00 00          mov    $0xc6,%eax
   b26e5:       49 89 ca                mov    %rcx,%r10
   b26e8:       0f 05                   syscall   ; Look THIS line
   b26ea:       72 01                   jb     b26ed <_thread_sys___syscall+0xd>
   b26ec:       c3                      retq
   b26ed:       64 89 04 25 20 00 00    mov    %eax,%fs:0x20
   b26f4:       00
   b26f5:       48 c7 c0 ff ff ff ff    mov    $0xffffffffffffffff,%rax
   b26fc:       c3                      retq
Disassembly of section .plt:

Interrupts above 20h communicate with the operating system or firmware [e.g., BIOS (Basic Input Output System present in ~ROM) has INT 13h, INT 10h and other.. which now conflict without issues with CPU exceptions, DOS had its interrupt(s) (INT 21h as an API and INT 20h only to terminate a program), Linux OS services kind of API to programs named in Unix "system call" was originally chosen on int 80h as long as processors operated in 32-bit mode, as well did other Unices for x86 architecture as 386/BSD.

Such a way to interface with the OS has a short opcode (no need to call far address... even though it can in some cases possibly be emulated by few other instructions (9C) pushf and call address specified at a memory location. However, emulating the call would enter the execution with lower privileges as protection mode separate the privilege on which code is executed).

There are way less than 257 classes of hardware signals to handle as the INT instruction in theory permits as its natural hardware signal design (one more than 256 is because INT 03 has two possible opcodes, the obvious CD 03 and the special INT3 single byte opcode CC to facilitate the way hardware breakpoint was injected originally into 8088 CPU by 8259 PIC, the leftover by signal handling is suitable as a global API to across-context-call code in memory, as intel later documented.

See also

  • A guide to Linux system calls (2016)
  • What happens if you use the 32-bit int 0x80 Linux ABI in 64-bit code?
  • Is syscall an instruction on x86_64?

Q: How to skip or disable SSL check for browsers in mac os? A:

As the information explicitly say: the site uses HSTS. This means the site was visited before and the browser cached the information that the site requests access by HTTPS only and does allow to skip certificate warnings. Thus there is explicitly no simple way around it - by design of HSTS. This is not specific to MacOS.

To work around this you need to make sure that the browser no longer remembers the site as using HSTS. How to do this depends on the specific browser (and not the OS). See here for some instructions, including instructions for Chrome which you seem to use.
